title: A Conspiracy of Credit, Part III: How the Greatest Fraud in Human History Happened - and What It Means for Private Credit Today
summary: Eisman explains securitization and mortgage-era due-diligence failures, then argues that software concentration, retail liquidity promises and insurer links create private-credit vulnerabilities. Documented underwriting misconduct supports his central historical concern, but several absolutes fail: MBS predates the 1980s, Denmark has a substantial 30-year fixed mortgage market, some due-diligence samples expanded, and consumer mortgages can be modified. Civil RMBS enforcement contradicts broad claims that nothing happened without settling particular criminal-referral outcomes. The 2027-2028 refinancing scenario remains unfinished; universal private-software valuation losses and undated credit-cycle predictions remain unproved.
assessment: Substantive article review with paragraph references. Distinguishes persuasive mechanisms from overgeneralized history, unverified market estimates, normative judgments and actual future deadlines. The specific criminal-accountability claim remains unresolved rather than rebutted with unrelated originator cases.
speaker_map_notes: Signed solo article by Steve Eisman. No guest attribution or inferred dialogue.
framework_points: Trace cash flows and loss seniority through securitization.
Separate collateral risk from repackaged security notional.
Inspect sampling design before extrapolating defects.
Distinguish civil enforcement from specific criminal referrals.
Match liquidity promises to underlying loan liquidity.
Separate public equity prices from private enterprise values.
Track maturity cohorts and sponsor equity support.
Include affiliated insurers in exposure mapping.
tools_and_charts: Clayton due-diligence samples and underwriting exceptions
transcript_cautions: This source is the complete substantive signed-in article, not an episode transcript. No player or full video transcript was available.
Use paragraph_references and source_locator; the normalization placeholders at zero are not speech timestamps.
Illustrative building and coupon figures are not treated as universal historical deal statistics.
The criminal-accountability discussion concerns Wall Street due-diligence conduct; scope is preserved.
Market-size, software and maturity estimates lack identified original datasets in the article.

claims.reason: Treasury's HAMP explicitly created mortgage modifications and payment reductions. Scale and servicing frictions do not mean impossibility.

evidence.title: Home Affordable Modification Program
evidence.finding: HAMP provided a mechanism for mortgage servicers to modify distressed homeowners loans and reduce monthly payments. Initial servicing constraints did not make consumer restructuring impossible.

claims.next_check: Compare legal mechanisms, capacity, take-up and modification outcomes.

claims.claim: Corporate borrowers can simply elect payment-in-kind interest or maturity extensions to defer distress.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Inspect covenants, PIK options, amendment thresholds and cash-flow sustainability.
claims.reason: These are possible contractual tools, but unilateral election requires existing rights; otherwise creditor consent is needed.
claims.next_check: Inspect covenants, PIK options, amendment thresholds and cash-flow sustainability.
claims.deductive_proof: A contract requiring cash interest and repayment on date T is not satisfied by unilaterally adding interest to principal or paying after T. PIK or extension is effective only if the contract permits it or the required parties amend it.

proof.derivation: A contract requiring cash interest and repayment on date T is not satisfied by unilaterally adding interest to principal or paying after T. PIK or extension is effective only if the contract permits it or the required parties amend it.

claims.claim: Private-equity and credit managers own insurers that invest in private-credit assets, creating additional connected exposures.

evidence.title: Private-credit vulnerabilities
evidence.finding: The estimated $1.5-2 trillion market has deepening bank, insurer and private-equity connections. Leverage, concentration, liquidity mismatches and limited data complicate assessment; current scale is untested in severe recession.

evidence.title: Report on vulnerabilities in private credit
evidence.finding: The monitoring framework includes subscription facilities, NAV/fund finance, borrower and fund leverage, retained risk and insurer affiliations.
